claim: Staphylococcus aureus is an opportunistic human pathogen that causes acute and chronic infections.
source: Here we describe a genetic program for cell-fate decision in the opportunistic human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus, which generates the phenotypic bifurcation of the cells into two genetically identical but different cell types during the course of an infection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: One S. aureus cell type promotes biofilm formation that contributes to chronic infections.
source: Whereas one cell type promotes the formation of biofilms that contribute to chronic infections, the second type is planktonic and produces the toxins that contribute to acute bacteremia.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: A second S. aureus cell type is planktonic and produces toxins that contribute to acute bacteremia.
source: Whereas one cell type promotes the formation of biofilms that contribute to chronic infections, the second type is planktonic and produces the toxins that contribute to acute bacteremia.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: A bimodal switch in the agr quorum sensing system antagonistically regulates the differentiation of two physiologically distinct cell types in S. aureus.
source: We identified a bimodal switch in the agr quorum sensing system that antagonistically regulates the differentiation of these two physiologically distinct cell types.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Extracellular signals affect the behavior of the agr bimodal switch and modify the size of specialized subpopulations in specific colonization niches.
source: We found that extracellular signals affect the behavior of the agr bimodal switch and modify the size of the specialized subpopulations in specific colonization niches.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Magnesium-enriched colonization niches cause magnesium binding to S. aureus teichoic acids and increase bacterial cell wall rigidity.
source: For instance, magnesium-enriched colonization niches causes magnesium binding to S. aureusteichoic acids and increases bacterial cell wall rigidity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Magnesium binding to teichoic acids triggers a genetic program that downregulates the agr bimodal switch.
source: This signal triggers a genetic program that ultimately downregulates the agr bimodal switch.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Colonization niches with different magnesium concentrations influence the bimodal system activity, which defines a distinct ratio between BRcell and DRcell subpopulations.
source: Colonization niches with different magnesium concentrations influence the bimodal system activity, which defines a distinct ratio between these subpopulations; this in turn leads to distinct infection outcomes in vitro and in an in vivo murine infection model.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Different magnesium concentrations in colonization niches lead to distinct infection outcomes in vitro and in an in vivo murine infection model.
source: Colonization niches with different magnesium concentrations influence the bimodal system activity, which defines a distinct ratio between these subpopulations; this in turn leads to distinct infection outcomes in vitro and in an in vivo murine infection model.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Cell differentiation generates physiological heterogeneity in clonal bacterial infections and helps determine distinct infection types.
source: Cell differentiation generates physiological heterogeneity in clonal bacterial infections and helps to determine the distinct infection types.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: S. aureus causes a broad range of diseases using diverse virulence factors.
source: Nosocomial pathogens often cause a broad range of diseases using diverse virulence factors, such as production of tissue-damaging toxins or production of adhesins during biofilm formation (Bush et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bush et al., 2011.

claim: S. aureus can cause acute bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia, and chronic biofilm-associated infections in prosthetic devices.
source: Staphylococcus aureus is one such pathogen that is able to cause different types of life-threatening infections in hospital settings, from acute bacteremia to endocarditis, pneumonia and chronic biofilm-associated infections in prosthetic devices (Otto, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Otto, 2012.

claim: Host-microbe interactions likely drive the cellular processes that enable S. aureus to provoke disparate types of infections.
source: The underlying cellular processes that enable S. aureus to provoke these disparate types of infections is likely driven by host-microbe interactions (Casadevall et al., 2011), in which specific, yet-to-be-described extracellular signals play a role to generate distinct, locally defined types of infections (Veening et al., 2008; López and Kolter, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Casadevall et al., 2011; Veening et al., 2008; López and Kolter, 2010.

claim: The agr quorum sensing program controls infection outcome in S. aureus.
source: In S. aureus, infection outcome is controlled by the agr quorum sensing program, which is autoactivated in response to the self-produced extracellular signal AIP (autoinducing peptide) (Recsei et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Recsei et al., 1986.

claim: AIP binds to the AgrC histidine kinase membrane receptor and activates its cognate regulator AgrA via phosphorylation.
source: AIP binds to the AgrC histidine kinase membrane receptor and activates its cognate regulator AgrA via phosphorylation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: AgrA~P induces changes in cellular gene expression that result in rapid bacterial dispersion in the host and acute bacteremia.
source: AgrA~P induces changes in cellular gene expression that results in rapid bacterial dispersion in the host and acute bacteremia (Thoendel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thoendel et al., 2011.

claim: Dispersion of S. aureus requires upregulation of surfactant phenol-soluble modulins (psmα and psmβ).
source: Dispersion of S. aureus requires upregulation of surfactant phenol-soluble modulins (psmα and psmβ), which are amphipathic small peptides that contribute to bacteria detachment (Li et al., 2009a; Peschel and Otto, 2013) and destabilize cell membranes, rendering them cytotoxic to host cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2009a; Peschel and Otto, 2013.

claim: Phenol-soluble modulins are amphipathic small peptides that contribute to bacteria detachment and are cytotoxic to host cells.
source: Dispersion of S. aureus requires upregulation of surfactant phenol-soluble modulins (psmα and psmβ), which are amphipathic small peptides that contribute to bacteria detachment (Li et al., 2009a; Peschel and Otto, 2013) and destabilize cell membranes, rendering them cytotoxic to host cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2009a; Peschel and Otto, 2013.

claim: Modulins are usually expressed during acute infections, as well as hemolytic toxins (hla, hlb, hlg) that facilitate tissue disruption during septicemia.
source: Modulins are usually expressed during acute infections, as well as hemolytic toxins (hla, hlb, hlg) that facilitate tissue disruption during septicemia (Recsei et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Recsei et al., 1986.

claim: Agr activation indirectly downregulates the icaADBC operon genes needed to synthesize the extracellular polysaccharide matrix (PNAG or PIA).
source: In contrast, agr activation indirectly downregulates the icaADBC operon genes needed to synthesize the extracellular polysaccharide matrix that protects cells within a biofilm (PNAG or PIA), as well as several adhesion proteins (SpA and other MSCRAMM proteins) responsible for cell aggregation/attachment during biofilm formation (Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988.

claim: Agr activation downregulates several adhesion proteins (SpA and other MSCRAMM proteins) responsible for cell aggregation/attachment during biofilm formation.
source: In contrast, agr activation indirectly downregulates the icaADBC operon genes needed to synthesize the extracellular polysaccharide matrix that protects cells within a biofilm (PNAG or PIA), as well as several adhesion proteins (SpA and other MSCRAMM proteins) responsible for cell aggregation/attachment during biofilm formation (Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988.

claim: Biofilms protect bacteria from antibiotics and host defenses.
source: Biofilms, which are associated with untreatable chronic infections, protect bacteria from antibiotics and host defenses (Lewis, 2008; Lopez et al., 2010; Nadell et al., 2009; Parsek and Singh, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lewis, 2008; Lopez et al., 2010; Nadell et al., 2009; Parsek and Singh, 2003.

claim: The S. aureus agr quorum sensing system antagonistically regulates the activation of planktonic and biofilm-associated lifestyles.
source: The S. aureus agr quorum sensing system antagonistically regulates the activation of planktonic and biofilm-associated lifestyles (Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988), which contribute to the development of acute and chronic infection outcomes, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988.

claim: The agr system is inhibited by the σB sigma factor.
source: Among those, the agr system is inhibited by the σB sigma factor (Bischoff et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bischoff et al., 2001.

claim: Activation of σB occurs during early stationary phase in response to distinct types of cellular stresses.
source: Activation of σB occurs during early stationary phase (Senn et al., 2005) in response to distinct types of cellular stresses (Geiger et al., 2014; Geiger and Wolz, 2014; Kästle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Senn et al., 2005; Geiger et al., 2014; Geiger and Wolz, 2014; Kästle et al., 2015.

claim: σB triggers a general stress response that affects expression of virulence and stress-response genes and indirectly represses agr.
source: σB triggers a general stress response that affects expression of a number of virulence and stress-response genes and indirectly represses agr (Thoendel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thoendel et al., 2011.

claim: σB antagonizes the influence of the agr system on virulence factor expression and biofilm formation.
source: Thus, σB antagonizes the influence of the agr system on virulence factor expression (Senn et al., 2005; Pané-Farré et al., 2006) and biofilm formation (Bischoff et al., 2001; Kullik et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Senn et al., 2005; Pané-Farré et al., 2006; Bischoff et al., 2001; Kullik et al., 1998.

claim: All agr-related reporters showed bimodal expression in S. aureus aggregates.
source: All reporters showed bimodal expression and indicated the bifurcation of two cell subpopulations in S. aureus aggregates, one with lower and another with higher fluorescence levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The bimodal expression pattern of agr-related reporters differed from the unimodal expression of the housekeeping and agr-independent gene dnaA.
source: This bimodal expression pattern differed from the unimodal expression of the housekeeping and agr-independent gene dnaA, used as control reporter (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Different S. aureus isolates showed bimodal expression of agr-related reporters.
source: Cultures of different S. aureus isolates showed bimodal expression of these reporters (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), which suggests that cell differentiation is a general phenomenon in S. aureus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cell differentiation is a general phenomenon in S. aureus.
source: Cultures of different S. aureus isolates showed bimodal expression of these reporters (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), which suggests that cell differentiation is a general phenomenon in S. aureus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different S. aureus isolates showed bimodal expression.

claim: Larger subpopulations of ica- and spa-expressing cells were observed in early developmental stages (~72 hr) compared to later growth stages (~120 hr).
source: Monitoring the temporal dynamics of the subpopulations that bifurcated during the development of the microbial aggregates from an initial inoculum in TSBMg revealed larger subpopulations of ica- and spa-expressing cells in early developmental stages (~72 hr; Figure 1B), compared to the size of these subpopulation at later growth stages (~120 hr).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The size of the subpopulations of psmα/β-expressing cells increased concomitantly with time.
source: In contrast, the size of the subpopulations of psmα/β-expressing cells increased concomitantly with time, consistent with the reported antagonistic regulation of ica/spa and psmα/β by agr (Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B and citations to Recsei et al., 1986; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Peng et al., 1988.

claim: Two distinct subpopulations of cells were identified: BRcells specialized in expressing ica, spa and other biofilm-related genes, and DRcells expressing psmα/β dispersion-related genes.
source: This approach indicated coexpression of ica with spa and of psmα with psmβ in two distinct cell subpopulations, showing the bifurcation of two distinct subpopulation of cells specialized in expressing ica, spa and other biofilm-related genes (BRcells) and cells expressing psmα/β dispersion-related genes (DRcells).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Once a certain AgrA~P threshold is reached in a cell, AgrA~P induces its own expression and these cells maintain high AgrA~P levels.
source: We hypothesize that, once a certain AgrA~P threshold is reached in a cell, AgrA~P induces its own expression and these cells maintain high AgrA~P levels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the bimodal behavior observed.

claim: Activation of the P3 promoter leads DRcells to specialize in dispersion and virulence.
source: Activation of the P3 promoter leads DRcells to specialize in dispersion and virulence.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of P3 in activating virulence genes.

claim: Cells that do not achieve the AgrA~P expression threshold needed to induce the positive feedback mechanism will not induce P3 promoter expression and will differentiate as biofilm-producing BRcell types.
source: In contrast, cells that do not achieve the AgrA~P expression threshold needed to induce the positive feedback mechanism will not induce P3 promoter expression. In these cells, genes normally repressed by AgrA~P will be upregulated, including biofilm-related genes, which licenses cells to differentiate as biofilm-producing BRcell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of the agr positive feedback loop.

claim: An orthogonal agr system in B. subtilis was genetically engineered to isolate the agr positive feedback loop from its native complex regulatory network.
source: To determine whether activation of the agr positive feedback loop is sufficient to generate bimodality in a bacterial population, we genetically engineered an orthogonal agr system in B. subtilis in which the agr positive feedback loop was isolated from its native complex regulatory network (Audretsch et al., 2013) and thus exempt from interference from additional staphylococcal regulatory inputs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Audretsch et al., 2013.

claim: The orthogonal system in B. subtilis does not express staphylococcal σB, and σB from B. subtilis did not interfere with the agr system.
source: The orthogonal system does not express staphylococcal σB, and σB from B. subtilis did not interfere with the agr system, since we detected similar reporter expression in wild type (WT) and ΔsigB strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), ensuring the absence of the agr inhibitory input signal.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of purified AIP to B. subtilis cultures activates AgrC sensor kinase, which phosphorylates the AgrA regulator, resulting in bimodal expression of Ppsmα-yfp or Ppsmβ-yfp reporters.
source: AIP addition activates AgrC sensor kinase, which phosphorylates the AgrA regulator. The AgrA~P active form binds the P2 promoter to express high AgrA~P levels and activate the positive feedback loop; this resulted in bimodal expression of chromosomally integrated Ppsmα-yfp or Ppsmβ-yfp reporters, with a cell subpopulation in which reporter expression increased during a transition in which cells switched from off to on.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the orthogonal system shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chromosomally integrated Pica-yfp and Pspa-yfp reporters did not activate in response to added AIP in the orthogonal system.
source: In contrast, chromosomally integrated Pica-yfp and Pspa-yfp reporters, which are not controlled directly by the AgrA~P, did not activate in response to added AIP.
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No fluorescence was detected in control experiments with strains lacking the AgrC-AgrA system, or when no AIP was added.
source: In a similar manner, we did not detect fluorescence in control experiments with strains lacking the AgrC-AgrA system, or when no AIP was added (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating that stochastic expression of these reporter genes does not account for bifurcation of the cell populations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The minimal agr genetic program harbored in the orthogonal system acts as an autonomous program for cell differentiation in bacterial populations.
source: These results indicate that the minimal agr genetic program harbored in the orthogonal system acts as an autonomous program for cell differentiation in bacterial populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the orthogonal system experiments.

claim: The P2-expressing cell subpopulation differentiated earlier and showed a more intense fluorescence signal in a larger cell subpopulation over time compared to the P3-expressing cells.
source: The P2-expressing cell subpopulation differentiated earlier, however, and showed a more intense fluorescence signal in a larger cell subpopulation over time compared to the orthogonal system that differentiated P3-expressing cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: P2 promoter is more sensitive than P3 to agr activation.
source: This result suggests that P2 promoter is more sensitive than P3 to agr activation, a characteristic feature of positive feedback loops in bimodal systems (Siebring et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to Siebring et al., 2012.

claim: The bimodal behavior of agr relies on the differential affinity of AgrA~P for P2 and P3 promoters.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesized that the bimodal behavior of agr and thus, cell differentiation in S. aureus, relies on the differential affinity of AgrA~P for P2 and P3 promoters.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on experimental observations.

claim: P2 activates the feedback loop at lower AgrA~P concentrations and only in a subpopulation of cells.
source: P2 thus activates the feedback loop at lower AgrA~P concentrations and only in a subpopulation of cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity of P2 and P3 promoters.

claim: Mathematical modeling and computational simulations showed that the correct combination of promoter rates sufficed to explain bimodal fluorescence distribution.
source: The correct combination of these promoter rates sufficed to explain bimodal fluorescence distribution.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: Simulations favored a model in which P2-activated positive feedback loop induces P3-driven bimodal expression in response to AIP concentration or autoactivation time.
source: Simulations favored a model in which P2-activated positive feedback loop induces P3-driven bimodal expression in response to AIP concentration or autoactivation time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E), suggesting that DRcells resulted from sequential P2 and P3 promoter activation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: At 4 hr post-AIP induction, a cell subpopulation that expressed P2 was detected; a fraction of this subpopulation activated P3 at later times (6 hr).
source: At 4 hr post-AIP induction, we detected a cell subpopulation that expressed P2; a fraction of this subpopulation activated P3 at later times (6 hr).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The subpopulation of P3-expressing cells increased over time until it expressed P2 and P3 promoters uniformly.
source: The subpopulation of P3-expressing cells increased over time until it expressed P2 and P3 promoters uniformly.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cells that expressed only the P3 promoter were not detected.
source: Cells that expressed only the P3 promoter were not detected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The molecular mechanism for bimodal gene expression relies on the differential AgrA~P affinity for P2 and P3 promoters.
source: The molecular mechanism for bimodal gene expression thus relies on the differential AgrA~P affinity for P2 and P3 promoters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dual orthogonal system experiments.

claim: BRcell and DRcell subpopulations are detected at different ratios in TSB and TSBMg cultures.
source: Once the agr switch responsible for BRcell and DRcell differentiation is activated, distinct extracellular cues can arise from the niche to feed into the agr bimodal switch and modulate its activity. For instance, BRcell and DRcell subpopulations are detected at different ratios in TSB and TSBMg cultures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments comparing TSB and TSBMg cultures.

claim: In TSBMg medium, qRT-PCR analysis showed increased expression of the σB-dependent stress gene asp23.
source: In TSBMg medium, qRT-PCR analysis showed increased expression of the σB-dependent stress gene asp23 (alkaline shock protein) (Gertz et al., 2000) (Figure 3A) and of staphyloxanthin, the pigment that gives S. aureus its typical yellow color and whose expression is regulated directly by σB (Gertz et al., 2000; Giachino et al., 2001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and supported by citations to Gertz et al., 2000; Giachino et al., 2001.

claim: TSBMg medium induced biofilm formation.
source: TSBMg medium also induced biofilm formation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Biofilm formation in TSBMg likely occurred via agr inhibition because the ΔsigB strain did not form biofilm and the biofilm formation phenotype was partially recovered in a ΔsigBΔagr double mutant.
source: Biofilm formation likely occurred via agr inhibition because the ΔsigB strain did not form biofilm and the biofilm formation phenotype was partially recovered in a ΔsigBΔagr double mutant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Mg2+ signaling cascade acts on agr downregulation via σB activation to increase BRcell subpopulation size.
source: Thus, the Mg2+ signaling cascade acts on agr downregulation via σB activation to increase BRcell subpopulation size.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Biofilm-associated S. aureus colonization generally occurs in Mg2+-enriched niches such as bone and kidney, in which chronic staphylococcal infections often develop.
source: This is consistent with the fact that biofilm-associated S. aureus colonization generally occurs in Mg2+-enriched niches such as bone and kidney, in which chronic staphylococcal infections often develop (Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012; Elin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012; Elin, 2010.

claim: Tissues unintentionally depleted of Mg2+ are prone to acute staphylococcal infections.
source: By contrast, tissues unintentionally depleted of Mg2+ are prone to acute staphylococcal infections, as Mg2+ sequestration from tissues due to tampon use was associated with an outbreak of staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome in women in the USA (Parsonnet et al., 1996; Schlievert, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parsonnet et al., 1996; Schlievert, 1985.

claim: Extracellular Mg2+ binds TA to increase cell wall rigidity.
source: The molecular mechanism whereby extracellular Mg2+ downregulates the agr bimodal switch relies on the capacity of magnesium to bind TA to increase cell wall rigidity (Heptinstall et al., 1970; Hughes et al., 1971), in turn causing agr downregulation via activation of the repressor σB.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heptinstall et al., 1970; Hughes et al., 1971.

claim: AFM detected greater rigidity in cells grown in TSBMg medium than those grown in TSB medium.
source: We detected greater rigidity in cells grown in TSBMg medium than those grown in TSB medium.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D using atomic force microscopy.

claim: In Mg2+-enriched growth conditions, extracellular Mg2+ binding complemented the cell wall rigidity defect in the ΔdltA mutant.
source: In Mg2+-enriched growth conditions, extracellular Mg2+ binding complemented the cell wall rigidity defect in this mutant, as TA-coordinated Mg2+ provided cell wall rigidity in the absence of the Dlt machinery.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Extracellular Mg2+ is incorporated to cell wall TA to increase cell wall rigidity.
source: These experiments indicate that extracellular Mg2+ is incorporated to cell wall TA to increase cell wall rigidity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFM experiments.

claim: Cells treated with sublethal doses of tunicamycin did not respond to Mg2+ and biofilm formation was inhibited.
source: In these conditions, cells treated with sublethal doses of tunicamycin, which inhibits TarO and thus teichoic acid synthesis at low concentrations (Swoboda et al., 2010; Campbell et al., 2011; Nunomura et al., 2010; Swoboda et al., 2009), did not respond to Mg2+ and biofilm formation was inhibited (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and supported by citations to Swoboda et al., 2010; Campbell et al., 2011; Nunomura et al., 2010; Swoboda et al., 2009.

claim: Strains with reduced tagB expression did not respond to Mg2+ and thus did not develop biofilms (low-tagB strain).
source: Strains with reduced tagB expression did not respond to Mg2+ and thus did not develop biofilms (low-tagB strain) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Strains with upregulated tagB became hypersensitive to extracellular Mg2+ and produced more robust biofilms (high-tagB).
source: In contrast, strains with upregulated tagB became hypersensitive to extracellular Mg2+ and produced more robust biofilms (high-tagB) even with Mg2+ traces that are present in regular TSB medium (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The low-tagB strain responded more weakly to extracellular Mg2+ than the high-tagB strain, with limited σB activation in both TSB and TSBMg conditions.
source: The low-tagB strain responded more weakly to extracellular Mg2+ than the high-tagB strain, with limited σB activation in both TSB and TSBMg conditions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The high-tagB strain was hypersensitive to extracellular Mg2+, with higher σB activation than the other strains in TSB.
source: In contrast, the high-tagB strain was hypersensitive to extracellular Mg2+, with higher σB activation than the other strains in TSB.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Extracellular Mg2+ stabilizes TA, increases cell wall rigidity and triggers the σB inhibitory signal responsible for downregulating the agr bimodal switch.
source: These results are consistent with our hypothesis that extracellular Mg2+ stabilizes TA, increases cell wall rigidity and triggers the σB inhibitory signal responsible for downregulating the agr bimodal switch.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Mg2+ in the colonization niche acts as a downregulatory signal, as it induces σB; activation of the agr switch becomes more difficult in these conditions and DRcell subpopulation size is reduced.
source: For instance, Mg2+ in the colonization niche acts as a downregulatory signal, as it induces σB; activation of the agr switch becomes more difficult in these conditions and DRcell subpopulation size is reduced (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Purified AIP added to cultures at various concentrations above threshold caused differentiation of a DRcell subpopulation that increased in parallel with AIP concentration but cell heterogeneity nonetheless remained detectable.
source: Purified AIP was added to Ppsmα-yfp or Ppsmβ-yfp reporter strain cultures at various concentrations above threshold concentration of ~10 μM usually found in cultures, which caused differentiation of a DRcell subpopulation that increased in parallel with AIP concentration but cell heterogeneity nonetheless remained detectable in cultures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: WT cultures in Mg2+-enriched growth conditions had a smaller DRcell subpopulation.
source: When we analyzed downregulation of the bimodal switch, WT cultures in Mg2+-enriched growth conditions had a smaller DRcell subpopulation (Figure 4A), whereas the ΔsigB mutant in TSB and TSBMg media differentiated a larger DRcell subpopulation than the WT strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ΔsigB mutant in TSB and TSBMg media differentiated a larger DRcell subpopulation than the WT strain.
source: When we analyzed downregulation of the bimodal switch, WT cultures in Mg2+-enriched growth conditions had a smaller DRcell subpopulation (Figure 4A), whereas the ΔsigB mutant in TSB and TSBMg media differentiated a larger DRcell subpopulation than the WT strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In both WT and ΔsigB mutant, BRcell and DRcell differentiation was detected.
source: Nevertheless, in both cases BRcell and DRcell differentiation was detected in the ΔsigB mutant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The low- and high-tagB strains showed larger and smaller DRcell subpopulations, respectively, in TSBMg although both subpopulations were detected.
source: Similarly, the low- and high-tagB strains, which are hypo- and hypersensitive to extracellular Mg2+, showed larger and smaller DRcell subpopulations, respectively, in TSBMg (Figure 4D) although both subpopulations were detected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the Δagr strain, expression of Ppsmα-yfp or Ppsmβ-yfp labeled reporters was not detected thus cell differentiation was inhibited in both TSB and TSBMg media.
source: According to the information we obtained using the agr orthogonal system and to confirm that the only means by which to lead the system into unimodal gene expression is by disrupting the agr positive feedback loop, we monitored DRcell differentiation in the Δagr strain. In this strain, expression of Ppsmα-yfp or Ppsmβ-yfp labeled reporters was not detected thus cell differentiation was inhibited in both TSB and TSBMg media (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In the absence of a functional agr feedback loop, no cell differentiation was detected and reporter expression was homogenous throughout the bacterial population.
source: In the absence of a functional agr feedback loop, we detected no cell differentiation and reporter expression was homogenous throughout the bacterial population.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The agr positive feedback loop must be active to trigger cell differentiation, and its activity is regulated by additional input cues that change the ratio of the specialized subpopulations.
source: These results show that the agr positive feedback loop must be active to trigger cell differentiation, and that its activity is regulated by additional input cues that change the ratio of the specialized subpopulations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in Figure 4.

claim: The mathematical model predicted that as an aggregate grows and expands, nutrients become limited in the older, central biofilm region, which has higher AIP levels and slow-dividing cells, which increases representation of the DRcell subpopulation.
source: Based on the morphological traits of the multicellular aggregates in different genetic backgrounds (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–G), the model predicted that as an aggregate grows and expands, nutrients become limited in the older, central biofilm region, which has higher AIP levels and slow-dividing cells, which increases representation of the DRcell subpopulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The most peripheral region of mature aggregates had a larger proportion of BRcells and a smaller proportion of DRcells.
source: In accordance with the mathematical predictions, the most peripheral region had a larger proportion of BRcells and a smaller proportion of DRcells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DRcells were enriched in the aggregate center.
source: DRcells were enriched in the aggregate center.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BRcells were highly represented in regions near the aggregate outer edge, where nutrient concentration is high.
source: BRcells were highly represented in regions near the aggregate outer edge, where nutrient concentration is high (Cramton et al., 2001), whereas DRcell representation was more prominent in the biofilm inner region, further from the nutrient source.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and supported by citation to Cramton et al., 2001.

claim: DRcell representation was more prominent in the biofilm inner region, further from the nutrient source.
source: BRcells were highly represented in regions near the aggregate outer edge, where nutrient concentration is high (Cramton et al., 2001), whereas DRcell representation was more prominent in the biofilm inner region, further from the nutrient source.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Enrichment of BRcells in newer and of DRcells in older biofilm regions suggests that staphylococcal cells respond differently to local input signal concentrations, and differentiate distinct DRcell:BRcell ratios in different biofilm regions.
source: These experiments showed enrichment of BRcells in newer and of DRcells in older biofilm regions, suggesting that the staphylococcal cells respond differently to local input signal concentrations, and differentiate distinct DRcell:BRcell ratios in different biofilm regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Genome-wide analysis showed similar genetic landscapes for DRcell and BRcell subpopulations, indicating that cell differentiation is not the result of accumulated mutations.
source: Genome-wide analysis showed similar genetic landscapes for DRcell and BRcell subpopulations, indicating that cell differentiation is not the result of accumulated mutations (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Comparison of the normalized gene expression profiles showed marked differences between the enriched subpopulation and its non-enriched counterpart, which suggested that a specific physiological state could be attributed to each particular cell type.
source: Comparison of the normalized gene expression profiles (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and Figure 6—source datas 2–4) and qRT-PCR validation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E) showed marked differences between the enriched subpopulation and its non-enriched counterpart, which suggested that a specific physiological state could be attributed to each particular cell type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E, and Figure 6—source datas 2–4.

claim: BRcells had a large number of upregulated genes, including sigB sigma factor, and of many biofilm-related genes as well as genes related to peptidoglycan turnover, cell division and DNA replication.
source: BRcells had a large number of upregulated genes, including sigB sigma factor, and of many biofilm-related genes as well as genes related to peptidoglycan turnover, cell division and DNA replication.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 49 tRNAs were upregulated in BRcells, which indicates the higher metabolic activity of BRcells and their physiological predisposition to proliferation.
source: In addition, 49 tRNAs were upregulated, which indicates the higher metabolic activity of BRcells and their physiological predisposition to proliferation (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: DRcells showed a smaller number of upregulated genes, which was attributed to lower gene expression activity potentially due to the lower physiological activity of this cell type.
source: DRcells showed a smaller number of upregulated genes, which we attributed to lower gene expression activity potentially due to the lower physiological activity of this cell type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Among the upregulated genes in DRcells, a notable number were related to toxin secretion and host invasion, such as the type-VII secretion system.
source: Among the few upregulated genes detected, we found a notable number related to toxin secretion and host invasion, such as the type-VII secretion system (Burts et al., 2005), as well as genes related to protecting bacterial cells from the immune system, such as the hssRS-htrAB hemin detoxification system (Stauff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and supported by citations to Burts et al., 2005; Stauff et al., 2007.

claim: DRcells showed upregulation of multi-drug efflux pumps that confer resistance to diverse antimicrobials, and of regulators such as graR and arsR.
source: We also detected upregulation of multi-drug efflux pumps that confer resistance to diverse antimicrobials, and of regulators such as graR and arsR, which positively control gene-related cell-wall antibiotic resistance and metal ion stress (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The expression of selected housekeeping genes in aggregates growing in TSBMg and TSB showed no differences.
source: In contrast, the expression of selected housekeeping genes in aggregates growing in TSBMg and TSB showed no differences (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F), suggesting that extracellular Mg2+ specifically influences the agr bimodal switch pathway rather than causing a global deregulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The DRcell subpopulation has lower metabolic activity than BRcell and is predisposed to resist different types of antimicrobials.
source: These results suggest that the DRcell subpopulation has lower metabolic activity than BRcell and is predisposed to resist different types of antimicrobials.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptomic data.

claim: Bacteria proliferated more efficiently in Mg2+-rich organs such as kidney.
source: The in vitro results correlated with the in vivo experiments; bacteria proliferated more efficiently in Mg2+-rich organs such as kidney.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Infected kidneys showed a bacterial load of 1010 CFU/g of tissue.
source: Infected kidneys showed a bacterial load of 1010 CFU/g of tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), and histological preparations of these organs showed large bacterial aggregates surrounded by immune cell infiltrates (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3), indicative of long-term colonization during septicemia (Prabhakara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation to Prabhakara et al., 2011.

claim: Histological preparations of infected kidneys showed large bacterial aggregates surrounded by immune cell infiltrates, indicative of long-term colonization during septicemia.
source: Infected kidneys showed a bacterial load of 1010 CFU/g of tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), and histological preparations of these organs showed large bacterial aggregates surrounded by immune cell infiltrates (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3), indicative of long-term colonization during septicemia (Prabhakara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3, and supported by citation to Prabhakara et al., 2011.

claim: Confocal microscopy analyses showed approximately three-fold more BRcells than DRcells in kidney aggregates.
source: Confocal microscopy analyses showed approximately three-fold more BRcells than DRcells in kidney aggregates (Figure 7C Figure 7—figure supplement 2), similar to levels detected in in vitro experiments; this was consistent with reports that kidneys are Mg2+ reservoirs in the body (Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012), and that 82% of patients with urinary catheterization develop long-term S. aureus infections (Muder et al., 2006).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and supported by citations to Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012; Muder et al., 2006.

claim: Infected hearts showed a bacterial load of 107 CFU/g of tissue.
source: On the other hand, infected hearts showed a bacterial load of 107 CFU/g of tissue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which suggested that S. aureus cells that colonized heart tissues proliferated less actively than those in kidney.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Infected hearts had a larger DRcell subpopulation, consistent with the lower metabolic activity, the lower proliferation rate of these cells in vitro and the lower Mg2+ concentration typically found in heart tissue.
source: Infected hearts had a larger DRcell subpopulation, consistent with the lower metabolic activity, the lower proliferation rate of these cells in vitro and the lower Mg2+ concentration typically found in heart tissue (Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012.

claim: Histological preparations of infected hearts revealed deposits of disperse cells with no immune cell infiltrates, which is indicative of acute bacteremia.
source: Histological preparations of infected hearts revealed deposits of disperse cells with no immune cell infiltrates (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3), which is indicative of acute bacteremia (McAdow et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3, and supported by citation to McAdow et al., 2011.

claim: As much as 60% of the total heart tissue-colonizing bacterial population consists of DRcells.
source: Confocal microscopy analysis showed that as much as 60% of the total heart tissue-colonizing bacterial population consists of DRcells (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2), as observed in in vitro experiments.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Kidneys showed a reduction in bacterial load when infected with the Mg2+-hyposensitive low-tagB strain.
source: Kidneys showed a reduction in bacterial load when infected with the Mg2+-hyposensitive low-tagB strain, although this strain colonized heart tissues more efficiently than S. aureus WT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The low-tagB strain colonized heart tissues more efficiently than S. aureus WT.
source: Kidneys showed a reduction in bacterial load when infected with the Mg2+-hyposensitive low-tagB strain, although this strain colonized heart tissues more efficiently than S. aureus WT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: qRT-PCR analyses verified that differences in bacterial load were associated with upregulation of key genes whose expression is restricted to DRcells (agrA, agrB and psmα/β) in low-tagB infections.
source: qRT-PCR analyses verified that these differences were associated with upregulation of key genes whose expression is restricted to DRcells (agrA, agrB and psmα/β), which suggests that infections with a low-tagB strain had marked representation of DRcells (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B–C.

claim: The Mg2+-hypersensitive high-tagB strain was able to infect kidneys more efficiently than the WT strain, concomitant with a reduced infection of heart tissues.
source: In contrast, the Mg2+-hypersensitive high-tagB strain was able to infect kidneys more efficiently than the WT strain, concomitant with a reduced infection of heart tissues.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: qRT-PCR analyses showed higher expression of genes related to BRcells (icaA, icaB and spa) in high-tagB infections, which suggested that the high-tagB strain differentiated a larger subpopulation of BRcells.
source: qRT-PCR analyses showed higher expression of genes related to BRcells (icaA, icaB and spa), which suggested that the high-tagB strain differentiated a larger subpopulation of BRcells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B–C.

claim: The infection pattern of the ΔsigB high-tagB strain resembled the low-tagB pattern in all the organs analyzed.
source: The infection pattern of this ΔsigB high-tagB strain resembled the low-tagB pattern in all the organs analyzed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Kidneys infected with the ΔsigB high-tagB strain showed a reduction in bacterial load, while heart tissues were colonized more efficiently.
source: Kidneys infected with this strain thus showed a reduction in bacterial load, while heart tissues were colonized more efficiently.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: qPCR analyses demonstrated higher expression of genes related to DRcells in infected kidneys and heart tissues of ΔsigB high-tagB strain, pointing to a larger number of DRcells in the infection of these strains.
source: qPCR analyses demonstrated higher expression of genes related to DRcells in infected kidneys and heart tissues, pointing to a larger number of DRcells in the infection of these strains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B–C.

claim: Infected livers showed comparable bacterial loads between low-tagB, high-tagB and ΔsigB high-tagB strains.
source: In addition, infected livers, which had a moderate of Mg2+ concentration (Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012), also showed comparable bacterial loads between low-tagB, high-tagB and ΔsigB high-tagB strains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A and supported by citations to Günther, 2011; Jahnen-Dechent and Ketteler, 2012.
